title: My Parents Raised Seven Children, Not Seven Copies
author: Isaac Hinkle
summary: This guest post by 21-year-old seminary student Isaac Hinkle, published on Anthony Bradley's fatherhood Substack, describes what it was like to be one of seven children whose parents treated each as a distinct person. Hinkle argues that his parents saw early that their children were different and chose homeschooling so they could nurture each one according to strengths and personality. He gives examples such as feeding his early reading with harder and more interesting books, signing him up for robotics, basketball and a lunch with the pastor when he asked theological questions at eight. His parents did not make the children do things they hated, but they also never let them settle for mediocrity, and his father often asked what he wanted to do with his life. The effects, he says, were direction, deeper mutual knowledge between parent and child, and a sense of having something valuable to contribute. He notes his parents were not perfect, but that the quiet, careful effort produced siblings who all walk with Christ in their own distinct ways.
points: Hinkle's central claim is that parents should recognise each child as a different person and tailor encouragement to that child rather than producing copies.
Following a child's interests, from reading to basketball to theology, while still pushing for excellence, builds both love of the activity and high standards.
Asking a ten-year-old what he wants to do with his life gave him a lens for testing activities and, just as usefully, learning what he did not want to do.
Individual attention produced deeper mutual knowledge, so a parent could read a moody teenager and send him to shoot baskets.
The effort required across seven children was great, yet the payoff was a family of distinct adults who felt they had something to contribute.
quotes: My parents, pretty early on, seem to have made the earth-shattering discovery that each of their children were completely different.
Thus, they chose the second option, homeschooling, so that they could nurture each of us in the ways they felt best suited to us and our unique personalities.
While my parents never made us do things we hated, they never let us settle for mediocrity. I liked basketball. My parents pushed me to get as good as I possibly could.
Again, if this seems like a lot of work for my parents, remember they have done this for ALL SEVEN CHILDREN. Each one is different.

We still tease my dad about how often he asked us as kids, “what do you want to do with your life?” It’s funny to picture that serious conversation between a father and his ten-year-old, but it really was such a helpful thing to ask.
I didn’t always know exactly what I wanted to do, but by exploring many things, I for sure knew what I DID NOT want to do. That knowledge was invaluable.
For example, if I was ever a moody teen, my mom would immediately tell me to go outside and practice basketball, because she knew that exercise made me feel better.
My parent’s attention and support made me feel like I had something valuable to contribute to the world and they were going to help me find it.
